title: The pi-Electron Approximation of Conjugation (Hückel Theory)
lead: Hückel theory keeps only the π electrons of a planar conjugated molecule, in orbitals built from one 2p<sub>z</sub> orbital on each carbon, and simplifies the secular determinant with four assumptions. Ethylene, with two carbons, is the first molecule it is applied to.
objectives: Demonstrate how Hückel's theory approximates the full molecular orbital picture of molecules by treating the $\sigma$-bonding and $\pi$-bonding networks independently.
notes: Written by Seymour Blinder and shared under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Figure 10.5.6's two images carry no credit in the book and are shared under the page's licence, and a hidden duplicate of one equation on the source page is left out.
exercise_notes: The book sets no exercise here. The one exercise is new and AI-written, with its answer computed from the β of Section 10.6; its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI. Numeric answers accept a 2% tolerance.

figures.original_caption: (a) The σ-bonded framework is formed by the overlap of two sets of singly occupied carbon sp2 hybrid orbitals and four singly occupied hydrogen 1s orbitals to form electron-pair bonds. This uses 10 of the 12 valence electrons to form a total of five σ bonds (four C–H bonds and one C–C bond). (b) One singly occupied unhybridized 2pz orbital remains on each carbon atom to form a carbon–carbon π bond. (Note: by convention, in planar molecules the axis perpendicular to the molecular plane is the z-axis.) (CC BY-NC; Ümit Kaya via LibreTexts)
Molecular orbitals demonstrating the sigma-pi separability of the $\pi$-bonding framework (blue) and the $\sigma$-bonding frameworks (red) of ethylene. (CC BY-NC; Ümit Kaya via LibreTexts)

exercises.source_id: The energy difference between the HOMO and LUMO is termed the HOMO–LUMO gap.
exercises.prompt: In Hückel theory ethylene's two π electrons fill $\pi_1$ at $\alpha + \beta$, and $\pi_2$ at $\alpha - \beta$ is empty. With the typical estimate $\beta = -75$ kJ/mol (Section 10.6), find (a) the HOMO–LUMO gap in kJ/mol and (b) the wavelength, in nm, of a photon whose energy equals that gap for one molecule.

parts.hint: The HOMO is π₁ and the LUMO is π₂.

answer.solution:
(a) The gap is $E_2 - E_1 = (\alpha - \beta) - (\alpha + \beta) = -2\beta = 2(75\ \text{kJ/mol}) = 150\ \text{kJ/mol}$.

(b) For one molecule, $\Delta E = \dfrac{1.50\times10^{5}\ \text{J/mol}}{6.022\times10^{23}\ \text{mol}^{-1}} = 2.49\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{(6.626\times10^{-34}\ \text{J s})(2.998\times10^{8}\ \text{m/s})}{2.49\times10^{-19}\ \text{J}} = 7.98\times10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 798\ \text{nm}$, in the near infrared. Ethylene in fact absorbs below 200 nm, in the far ultraviolet: with electron repulsion left out, Hückel theory badly underestimates the gap, as the note on its limitations warns.

footnotes.html: The second framework is the $\pi$-bonding framework: the two are the $\sigma$-bonding and the $\pi$-bonding frameworks.
Each atomic orbital has its own coefficient: $|\psi_1\rangle = a_1|2s\rangle + a_2|2p_x\rangle + a_3|2p_y\rangle + a_4|1s_a\rangle$.
The coefficients of the hybrid are the $\{b_i\}$, each orbital with its own: $|sp^2_1\rangle = b_1|2s\rangle + b_2|2p_x\rangle + b_3|2p_y\rangle$.
Both frameworks are drawn in Figure 10.5.1: the $\sigma$ framework in part (a) and the $\pi$ bond from the $2p_z$ orbitals in part (b).
The resonance integrals are the elements with $i \neq j$.

steps.tex: \mk{M}{\begin{bmatrix} \kalphaH - \kE S_{11} & \kbetaH - \kE S_{12} \\ \kbetaH - \kE S_{21} & \kalphaH - \kE S_{22} \end{bmatrix}} \mk{c}{\begin{bmatrix} c_1 \\ c_2 \end{bmatrix}} = 0

steps.cap: Dividing both equations by $\beta$ leaves their solutions unchanged.

assumes.text: Homogeneous equations have a solution other than $c_1 = c_2 = 0$ only if their determinant is zero.

steps.cap: A $2 \times 2$ determinant is the product of its diagonal less the product of its other two entries.

nodes.note: The book prints $E=\alpha -\pm 1\times \beta$ on the way; with $x = \pm 1$ in $E = \alpha - x\beta$ it is $E = \alpha \mp \beta$.

steps.cap: Since $\beta$ is negative, the lower energy is $\alpha + \beta$, which is $x = -1$.

nodes.note: The book prints $|\psi_1 \rangle = N_1 (\phi_1 \rangle + | \phi_2 \rangle )$, the first ket missing its bar.

The book prints “for the higher energy molecular orbital ($x=-1$)”: the higher energy, $\alpha - \beta$, belongs to $x = +1$. It also prints $\psi_2 \rangle$ and $(\phi_1 \rangle$, the kets missing their bars.

steps.cap: Both orbitals are $N(|\phi_1\rangle \pm |\phi_2\rangle)$, with $N = N_1$ or $N_2$; for real orbitals the two cross terms are equal.
